timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: What exactly happens at Layer 2 of the network?

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Layer 2 is Ethernet — frames, MAC addresses, and switches. It's how devices talk on the same local network.

timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: MAC addresses are unique, right? So that's secure?

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: MAC addresses are unique in hardware, but trivially spoofed in software. Anyone can pretend to be any device.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: ARP spoofing. You send fake ARP replies telling the network that your MAC is the gateway. All traffic flows through you.

timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: And the network just believes it?

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: ARP was designed for trust. There's no authentication. It believes whatever it hears first or most often.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: You flood a switch with fake MAC addresses. It runs out of memory, switches to hub mode, and broadcasts everything to everyone.

timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: That sounds like a nightmare. Can switches defend against this?

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Port security limits MACs per port. DHCP snooping and Dynamic ARP Inspection validate traffic. But they must be configured explicitly.

timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: So most networks don't have these defenses by default?

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Most don't. Layer 2 security is the most neglected layer in enterprise networks.
